rewritten_text:
When I returned, I found this letter from my father:

"My dear Victor,

"You have probably been waiting eagerly for a letter setting the date for your return. At first I thought of writing just a few lines to tell you when I expected you. But that would be kindness turned cruel, and I cannot do it. Imagine, my son, arriving in the hope of a happy welcome and finding only tears and misery. Yet how can I tell you what has happened? Being away cannot have made you indifferent to our happiness or sorrow. How can I hurt a son I have not seen for so long? I want to prepare you for this dreadful news, but I know that is impossible. Even now you must be scanning the page for the words that will tell you.

"William is dead! That sweet child whose smile warmed and delighted me, so gentle and so cheerful! Victor, he has been murdered!

"I will not try to comfort you. I will simply explain what happened.

"Last Thursday, May 7, I went walking in Plainpalais with my niece and your two brothers. The evening was warm and peaceful, so we stayed out longer than usual. It was already growing dark when we thought of going home. Then we noticed that William and Ernest, who had walked ahead, were nowhere in sight. We sat down to wait for them. Soon Ernest appeared and asked whether we had seen his brother. They had been playing together, he said, when William ran off to hide. Ernest searched without finding him, then waited a long time, but William never came back.

"This worried us, and we kept searching until nightfall. Then Elizabeth suggested he might have gone home. He was not there. We went out again with torches, for I could not rest while thinking of my dear boy lost outside in the damp night air. Elizabeth was also terribly distressed. At about five in the morning I found my beautiful child. The evening before he had been healthy and lively; now he lay discoloured and still upon the grass. A mark from the murderer's finger showed on his neck.

"We brought him home, and the anguish on my face told Elizabeth the truth. She desperately wanted to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she insisted. Entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined his neck, clasped her hands, and cried, 'Oh God!

Their arrival seemed to kindle a fire in the heart of Saint Antoine. It spread quickly as they passed, flaring in the faces at nearly every door and window. Yet nobody followed them. When they entered the wine shop, no one spoke, though every man's eyes turned toward them.

"Good day, gentlemen!" Monsieur Defarge said.

Perhaps this was a signal allowing everyone to speak. A chorus of "Good day!" answered him.

"Bad weather, gentlemen," Defarge said, shaking his head.

Each man looked at his neighbour. Then they all lowered their eyes and sat in silence, except for one who rose and left.

"My wife," Defarge said loudly to Madame Defarge, "I've travelled several leagues with this good road repairer, whose name is Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half's journey from Paris. He's a good fellow, this road repairer called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!"

A second man got up and went out. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road repairer called Jacques. He removed his blue cap to greet the company and drank. Inside the front of his blouse he carried some rough, dark bread. Between drinks he took bites of it, sitting and chewing near Madame Defarge's counter. A third man rose and left.

Defarge refreshed himself with some wine, though he drank less than his guest, since wine was no unusual luxury for him. Then he waited while the countryman finished his breakfast. He looked at nobody, and nobody looked at him now, not even Madame Defarge. She had picked up her knitting and was busy with it.

"Have you finished eating, my friend?" he asked when enough time had passed.

"Yes, thank you."

"Come along, then. I'll show you the room I said you could stay in. It will suit you perfectly."

They went from the wine shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, and from the stairs into an attic. Once, a white-haired man had sat there on a low bench, bending forward and working busily at making shoes.

The white-haired man was gone. Instead, the three men who had left the shop separately were waiting. One small connection linked them with the white-haired man now far away: they had once watched him through cracks in the wall.

Defarge carefully closed the door and lowered his voice.

"Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness whom I, Jacques Four, met by arrangement.

He got up and left with my nurse; a moment afterward my father came into the room.

At that instant nothing could have afforded me greater joy than his arrival. I reached a hand towards him and exclaimed,

"You are safe, then—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?"

My father soothed me by assuring me that they were well. He sought to revive my broken spirits by speaking of those so dear to my heart, but soon recognized that a prison could scarcely harbour cheerfulness. "What a dwelling this is, my son!" he said, surveying with sadness the barred windows and the room's miserable condition. "You went abroad in pursuit of happiness, yet some fatal power seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—"

The mention of my unhappy, murdered friend stirred feelings too violent for my weakness, and I wept.

"Alas, Father, yes," I answered. "Some dreadful destiny overshadows me, and I am compelled to live until I fulfil it. Otherwise I surely would have died beside Henry's coffin."

Our conversation could not continue long, for my uncertain health required every possible precaution to preserve my calm. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted that excessive effort must not exhaust my strength. Nevertheless, my father's presence was to me the presence of a benevolent angel, and my health slowly returned.

As the sickness faded, a dark and oppressive melancholy engulfed me, beyond the power of anything to dispel. Clerval's image remained constantly before my eyes, ghastly in his murdered state. More than once these reflections agitated me so severely that my friends feared a dangerous return of the illness. Alas, why had they sustained a life so wretched and abhorred? Surely so that I might accomplish the destiny now approaching its conclusion. Soon—very soon—death will quiet these throbbings and release me from the immense burden of anguish pressing me into the dust. In carrying out the sentence of justice, I too shall find repose. Then, however, death seemed remote, though the desire for it never left my thoughts. Often I sat for hours without speech or movement, longing for some tremendous upheaval whose ruins might bury both me and my destroyer.

The season for the assizes drew near. Three months of imprisonment had already passed, and despite my continuing weakness and constant risk of relapse, I had to journey almost a hundred miles to the county town where the court assembled. Mr. Kirwin undertook the entire business of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence.
